items.name: Slide Hampton
items.summary: Bryant recalled that Slide Hampton was in the trombone section on one of Liston's own record dates, which Liston acknowledged as 'a different Company altogether'; after her stroke Liston said she had tried turning her trombone around to blow it like Slide Hampton, without success.
items.one_liner: had him in her trombone section on record
items.her_quote: I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t
items.bryant_quote: But you had two separate ’bone sections on two different record dates. One was around Christmas time – they both were around Christmas time – one around the 22nd, one around the 24th. One you had Slide Hampton, Frank Rehak.

more_her_quotes.quote: Oh. That was a different Company altogether. I forgot about that.

items.notes: Name also appears in Bryant block 295988 (record-date 'bone section), which is not in mention_block_ids. Liston's 'different Company' reply is a loose acknowledgement, not an explicit confirmation. The 296174 remark refers to Hampton's turned-around (left-handed) way of holding the horn; the transcript itself does not explain it.

items.name: Gloria Lynne
items.summary: Liston said she wrote string arrangements and original ballads for Gloria Lynne's 1959 record, had Quincy Jones conduct the session when she was sick, and contrasted writing for Lynne's ballad soul with Dinah Washington's.
items.one_liner: wrote the string arrangements for her 1959 record
items.her_quote: Dinah – soul, soul, soul, but Gloria’s soul too, but it’s a different way. They come after me differently. I don’t know how to say it. When I write for Dinah – uh. And when I write for Gloria – it’s oo.

more_her_quotes.quote: Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy [Jones] and he conducted for me, but all of the arrangements are mine – almost all of them.
So I’ve been writing for strings as long as I’ve been writing for horns.
I would write the same way for Gloria Lynne – if I wrote for Dinah – one of those arrangements for Dinah, I would write the same way for Gloria Lynne, but she would sing it differently.
I feel like it’s the song, not the singer, makes the difference.

items.notes: Liston raised Lynne herself (296228, 296272, 296282). Bryant adds (296299) that Liston brought songs to Lynne and taught her some of them; Liston said 'Yeah.' The year 1959 is Bryant's (296273, 296283, 296295) and was not disputed.

items.name: Fife
items.notes: Not a person: 'Fife?' is Bryant guessing which instrument plays the high line on the 1973 Little Niles recording; Liston answered 'It wasn’t none of those things' and said it was a mouthpiece.

items.name: Jon Faddis
items.summary: Bryant guessed that the high line on the 1973 Little Niles track might be a trumpeter such as Jon Faddis; Liston replied that it was a mouthpiece and said nothing about Faddis.
items.notes: Mentioned only as Bryant's passing guess ('Jon Faddis or somebody'). No relation is established.

items.name: Pam's Waltz
items.notes: Not a person: 'Pam’s Waltz' is a Randy Weston tune that Liston said they record every time, along with Little Niles (296264).

items.name: Tanjah
items.notes: Not a person: 'Tanyah' / 'Tanjah' is the 1973 Randy Weston album that the Little Niles version came from (Bryant, 296241 and 296281).

items.name: Minnie (surname transcribed '?Morris')
items.identity_note: 'Morris' is half of the transcriber's uncertain guess '[?Moore ?Morris]' for this Minnie's surname. It is very probably Minnie Hightower (Liston's schoolmate in Mrs Hightower's Melodic Dots, identified in the next photograph in 296332). Duplicate of the 'Moore' entry, 104490.
items.summary: Looking at a photograph of her youth band from about 1938, Liston said she knew everyone in it except the drummer and a tall saxophonist, and named Minnie, whose surname the transcriber could only guess.
items.one_liner: named her in a youth-band photograph
items.her_quote: Everybody except the drummer, and I don’t know who the tall saxophonist is, but the rest of them I know. That’s me. Minnie – Minnie
items.notes: Name fragment from a bracketed guess. Merge with 104490 ('Moore') and probably with the Minnie Hightower entry. The year comes from 296320–296322 (Liston: '’38 or something like that').

items.name: Minnie (surname transcribed '?Moore')
items.identity_note: 'Moore' is half of the transcriber's uncertain guess '[?Moore ?Morris]' for this Minnie's surname. It is very probably Minnie Hightower (Liston's schoolmate in Mrs Hightower's Melodic Dots, identified in the next photograph in 296332). Duplicate of the 'Morris' entry, 104489.
items.summary: Looking at a photograph of her youth band from about 1938, Liston said she knew everyone in it except the drummer and a tall saxophonist, and named Minnie, whose surname the transcriber could only guess.
items.one_liner: named her in a youth-band photograph
items.her_quote: Everybody except the drummer, and I don’t know who the tall saxophonist is, but the rest of them I know. That’s me. Minnie – Minnie
items.notes: Name fragment from a bracketed guess. Merge with 104489 ('Morris') and probably with the Minnie Hightower entry.

items.name: Prince Harris
items.summary: Bryant pointed out Prince Harris in a photograph of Liston's youth band from about 1938, and Liston recognised him.
items.one_liner: recognised him in her youth-band photograph
items.notes: Bryant supplies the surname. Liston had already said she knew everyone in the photo except the drummer and a tall saxophonist (296312). Being in the same band is inferred from the photo.

items.name: Elvira (Vi) Redd
items.identity_note: Elvira is Vi Redd (born Elvira Redd). Bryant's 'Elvira – Vi Redd’s brother' (296319) ties the name to Vi Redd. Probably the same person as any separate 'Vi Redd' entry.
items.summary: Liston named Elvira (Vi Redd) in a photograph of her youth band from about 1938, and earlier said that she, Minnie Hightower and Alice Young were the girls she was close to in Mrs Hightower's band.
items.one_liner: was in miss hightower's youth band with her
items.her_quote: Alice Young. Those three, we were close.
items.notes: The 295549 quote answers Bryant's 'besides Minnie and Vi Redd?', so 'those three' are Minnie, Vi Redd and Alice Young. Upstream's 'mothers were friends' evidence belongs to an unnamed trumpeter (296318), not to Elvira. Merge with the Vi Redd entry if one exists.

items.name: His mother
items.notes: Not a named person. It refers to the mother of a trumpeter in the c. 1938 photograph whose name Liston could not recall: 'His mother and my mother used to be friends.' (296318). From the order of turns, that trumpeter may be Buddy Redd, Vi Redd's brother (296319), but this is unconfirmed.

items.name: Buddy Redd
items.summary: According to the transcriber's summary, Liston and Bryant identified Buddy Redd, Vi Redd's brother, in a photograph of Liston's youth band from about 1938.
items.one_liner: pictured with her in a youth-band photograph
items.notes: The name appears only in the bracket '[They identify Melba and Buddy Redd.]' inside Bryant's turn, followed by Bryant's 'Elvira – Vi Redd’s brother.' He may be the trumpeter Liston could not name, of whom she said 'His mother and my mother used to be friends.' (296318). If so, their families were friends, but the transcript does not make that link explicit. Check against the recording.

items.name: Ross Snyder (playground)
items.notes: Not a person: Ross Snyder is the Los Angeles playground where Liston's youth band practised ('We practiced at the Ross Snyder playground', 295547). 'This is Ross Snyder.' (296326) identifies the setting of the second photograph. The following 'I liked him' refers to a different man she was trying to identify, not to Ross Snyder.

items.name: Lorenzo
items.summary: When Bryant identified Lorenzo in an early photograph, Liston said she knew him as a trumpet player and was surprised to hear he played saxophone, and she did not know that Alice Young had been his pianist until he died.
items.one_liner: knew him as a trumpet player
items.her_quote: I don’t know how he’s playing saxophone, because I know him as a trumpet player.
items.notes: Identified by Bryant inside a bracket ('[identifies Lorenzo.]'). His surname is never given. Liston's 'I liked him. Not then. Maybe 15 years later. I can’t remember his name.' (296326) may refer to this same man, since Bryant names Lorenzo in the very next turn, but that is not certain, so it is not quoted here.

items.name: Robert Ross
items.summary: According to the transcriber's summaries, Liston thought an unidentified man in an early photograph was Robert Ross, Bryant produced another photograph showing Ross, and Ross appears with Minnie and Alice in a third photograph.
items.notes: Appears only in transcriber brackets (296332, 296337). Liston's guess at the name implies she knew him, but nothing beyond that is recorded.

items.name: Clifford Burden Jr.
items.identity_note: Two people are folded together. 'Clifford, Jr.' is Minnie Hightower and Clifford Burden's son, a preacher (Bryant, 296337). The bare 'Clifford' in the same block's bracket ('…Robert Ross, and Clifford in a pseudo-Hawaiian setting') is in a 1930s photograph, so it must be Clifford Burden Sr. (296333), whom Liston knew ('Oh yeah. He and Minnie both dead, huh?').
items.summary: Bryant said that Minnie Hightower's son Clifford Jr., now a preacher, had the box of photographs they were looking at; Liston said nothing about him.
items.notes: Upstream wrongly called him the son of Liston's ex-husband. Bryant's 'Minnie’s ex-husband – widow' refers to Minnie's widower. The 'Clifford' surface form should go to Clifford Burden Sr.

items.name: Horn players
items.notes: Not a person: generic advice to young musicians ('Horn players, get someone to take a pattern off of.', 296358).

items.name: DIVA
items.notes: Not a person: Diva (DIVA) is the all-female big band. Bryant mentions an unnamed San Francisco trombonist who 'was with Diva' (296420). Liston does not respond to it.

items.name: Janice Robinson
items.identity_note: Wikidata Q28485945 (American trombonist, b. 1951) fits Bryant's 'Such a beautiful trombonist'.
items.summary: Liston said the trombonist Janice Robinson had been in her band, had recently called to talk about taking up the horn again, and that she would call Robinson when she returned to New York.
items.her_quote: No. She was with me. She called me the other day.

more_her_quotes.quote: She was talking about taking up the horn again.
I told her I was coming back there and I would call her when I came back there.

items.notes: 'She was with me' is read as membership in Liston's band. The band is not named in this passage. Bryant adds that Robinson married and put the horn down; Liston said 'Yeah.' (296431).

items.name: Bu Pleasant
items.summary: Bryant recalled the all-women group Liston led with Bu Pleasant, and Liston agreed, describing how it worked around New York and went to China before she began replacing the women with men; she later named Bu Pleasant, a saxophonist, among the women musicians she cared about.
items.one_liner: led her all-women band on the china trip
items.bryant_quote: And what about the group that you had with Boo – Boo Pleasant, when you guys went to – Bermuda?

more_her_quotes.quote: We worked and worked all around New York and then we went to China.
Um-hmm. And I started weeding them out, one-by-one.

items.notes: Also spelled 'Boo Pleasant' (295782) and 'Bu' (295976), which are not in surface_forms. Bryant says Bermuda while Liston says China. The 'early 1980s' date comes from Bryant's 'at the beginning of the ’80s' (295782). Whether Liston led the group is inferred from her 'Melba Liston and Company, that was all the time' (295787).

items.name: Wilene Martin
items.summary: Bryant suggested Wilene Martin when Liston was naming women musicians; Liston's reply ('No, but she – all the . . .') is unfinished and establishes nothing about her.
items.notes: Liston's 'No' may mean that Martin was not the person she was thinking of, or may be a broken start. It is ambiguous.

items.name: Fostina Dixon
items.identity_note: Wikidata Q24036299 (American jazz musician, b. 1956) is plausible. Nothing in the transcript contradicts it.
items.summary: When Bryant named Fostina Dixon among the women musicians of the day, Liston agreed and said that all of them were having a hard time and that something had to be organised for the women.
items.one_liner: named among the women she wanted to help
items.her_quote: Yeah. All them. They’re – we got to get – they’re having a bitch of a time. We got to get something together for the girls.
items.notes: Liston's quote is about the women as a group. Any direct contact with Dixon is not established here.

items.name: Terri Lyne Carrington
items.summary: Liston raised 'a drummer' among the promising women musicians, Bryant supplied the name Teri Lyne Carrington, and Liston agreed, adding that they had to go back East.
items.one_liner: named among the promising women players
items.her_quote: And who else? I know they got to get out and go back East.
items.notes: The transcript spells it 'Teri Lyne Carrington'. The usual spelling is Terri Lyne Carrington. No upstream QID. Liston's quote is about the young women in general.

items.name: Stacey Rowles
items.summary: Bryant listed Stacey Rowles, Jimmie Rowles's daughter, as a young woman trumpet player in Los Angeles; Liston did not respond about her.
items.notes: Mentioned only in Bryant's long list (296492).

items.name: Ann Patterson
items.identity_note: Wikidata Q30693860 (saxophonist and bandleader, b. 1946) matches Bryant's description and the transcriber's bracketed name.
items.summary: Bryant described, without recalling her name, the reed player who took over a big band and plays with Maiden Voyage; the transcriber supplied the name Ann Patterson, and Liston did not respond about her.
items.notes: The name appears only as a transcriber's bracket inside Bryant's turn (296492).

items.name: Maiden Voyage
items.notes: Not a person: 'Maiden' is the first half of 'Maiden Voyage', the women's big band that Bryant mentions. The name runs across a page break (296492–296493).

items.name: Ben Loves Lu
items.notes: Not a person: 'Ben Loves Lu' is the tune Liston chose to close the interview, 'dedicated to my mom and her man, her husband' (296510). It is named for her mother Lucille and her mother's husband Ben, who is not otherwise identified.
